title: Sanhedrin
summary: A conventional label for Jewish councils represented by Greek synedrion terminology in late Second Temple sources, whose composition, jurisdiction, meeting forms, and institutional continuity remain debated.
historical_context: Josephus and the New Testament attest councils and assemblies of rulers, elders, priests, and scribes under Hasmonean and Roman rule. The evidence does not justify one unchanged seventy-one-member body operating identically in every passage.
ancient_near_east_context: The operative comparison is Hellenistic and Roman civic and provincial council practice, not generic Ancient Near Eastern judges or monarchy.
hebraic_worldview: Council scenes concern communal judgment, Torah, temple authority, public order, and accountability under both divine claims and imperial constraints.
second_temple_context: The Gospels and Acts use council language for Jerusalem hearings involving high priests, chief priests, elders, scribes, and rulers; source-specific composition and jurisdiction must be preserved.
canonical_context: Passion narratives and Acts hearings use council settings in distinct literary arguments. Later rabbinic court descriptions cannot automatically be read back into these scenes.
literary_context: Mark, Matthew, Luke, John, and Acts name different combinations of leaders and use council scenes to advance passion, witness, and trial narratives.
covenantal_significance: The council scenes depict contested claims to faithful judgment and communal protection under foreign rule; they should not authorize collective blame.
original_audience: Readers of Gospel passion accounts and Acts hearings who need cautious institutional rather than harmonized courtroom reconstruction.
historical_setting: Jerusalem under Hasmonean, Herodian, and early Roman rule, with changing local and imperial jurisdictions.
canonical_role: The record anchors council passages and directs historical reconstruction to the source-bounded priesthood and group evidence clusters.

related_objects.notes: Priestly authority, Josephus, and source-specific council cautions.

scripture_references.notes: High priest, chief priests, elders, scribes, and council in the hearing narrative.

interpretive_notes.note: Greek synedrion can denote a council or meeting; references in different narratives should not automatically be harmonized into one continuously constituted seventy-one-member court.
Later rabbinic court descriptions are important reception evidence but cannot by themselves settle the composition and jurisdiction of every pre-70 Jerusalem council.

common_questions: Does every New Testament council scene describe the same body?
